THE COMPUTER CAN FEEL THE ENGINE.

Follow
the pulses.

An engine changes the vehicle’s velocity. Accelerometers turn that change into pulses. The original Apollo computer counts them.

Try freefall, add thrust, then tilt the vehicle. Gravity changes velocity but produces no accelerometer pulses.

01

Choose the control source

Choose an experiment to load the verified flight program.

Manual mode boots the full computer and displays PIPA counts with V16 N21. FLATOUT runs a bounded test of the original throttle command, then services hardware counters only.

Keyboard: W/S throttle up/down; A/D tilt left/right. FLATOUT keeps control of throttle; A/D still works. A 0.20 s lag comes from the flight program’s throttle constants; the first-order response here is a teaching approximation. Change it to compare response.

02

What the computer counts

PIPAX / 0037   —
PIPAY / 0040   —
PIPAZ / 0041   —

One pulse represents 0.0585 m/s of thrust-driven velocity change. Fractional pulses accumulate. Raw words are octal; signed counts use the AGC’s one’s-complement arithmetic.

03

Watch the throttle drive

No command loaded.

FLATOUT sets THRUST (0055) and channel 014 bit 4. External drive clocks diminish the counter at 3,200 pulses/s; the original core emits POUT, MOUT and ZOUT. This experiment maps 4,096 positive pulses to full simulated travel.

04

The original display

Choose manual mode to boot
V16 N21 / PIPA monitor.

The manual experiment uses genuine keyboard packets and DSKY output. The isolated FLATOUT test stops before its return path and does not run the display or guidance Executive.

HARDWARE DEMONSTRATION · The rope is unchanged. FLATOUT entry registers are seeded by a diagnostic harness. No autonomous landing guidance is active.
WHAT THIS ESTABLISHES

A real path through the computer.

Sensor input uses the emulator’s unprogrammed PINC/MINC counter packets. Engine drive uses DINC and the actual output packets. The manual mode executes the flight software; the FLATOUT mode executes the preserved command instructions before counter-only service.

Reset between comparisons. Each experiment starts 600 m above a flat surface at −20 m/s, with 2,000 kg of fuel. These initial conditions are chosen for teaching. The model stops at contact or after 120 seconds.

WHAT STILL NEEDS CONNECTING

Navigation before landing.

The stable frame is held fixed: X is vertical, Y is out of plane, Z is downrange. This is not Apollo’s mission alignment. Radar, attitude sensing, lunar rotation and mission pad loads remain to be implemented. FLATOUT is an actuator test, not P63 or P66 guidance.
